gap: No result ChatGPT got gives a range figure tied to a battery size. Club Car's own Onward spec page rates the base 4.0 kWh HP Lithium pack at 20–35 miles new and 18–30 miles after four years, against 35–55 and 30–50 miles for the 7.0 kWh XR pack. No independent lab has published a measured range for any factory lithium cart, so the only first-hand figures come from named owners (for example, Homer49 drove 31.3 miles on an E-Z-GO RXV ELiTE using just under half the battery).
standout_why: Club Car's golf-carts page, which ChatGPT cited (clubcar.com/en-us/personal/golf-carts), lists only prices and speed ('Up to 19mph'), with no kWh, range or weight. Club Car's lithium-ion page, in the results but not cited, lists no range, kWh, charge time or warranty. The T&T inventory pages that ChatGPT cited returned no specs at all when opened. ChatGPT's own answer gave a generic '30–60 miles' that names no cart or pack. None of these pages separates the 4.0 kWh pack from the 7.0 kWh pack, gives the four-year fade, or quotes any measured or owner-observed range. RTINGS, Notebookcheck, Consumer Reports and magazine labs don't test golf carts, so no lab figure exists that could tip the pick on its own.
decides: It doesn't change which brand to buy, but it does decide which pack to choose. 'Club Car Onward Lithium from $11,299' could mean the base 4.0 kWh pack, which Club Car itself says drops to 18–30 miles after four years. A shopper who needs more than about 30 miles per charge should price the 7.0 kWh XR pack. E-Z-GO publishes no range for its ELiTE carts, so the only real-world figure for them is an owner's: Homer49's 31.3 miles using just under 50% on an RXV ELiTE (2021). The Onward lithium curb weight of 797 lb against 1,070 lb for lead-acid confirms lithium's weight advantage.
